lesson.title: Moeder, Vader & Leraar
lesson.subtitle: family words and what people do

hook.title: Family and Work
hook.content: Moeder, vader, broer, zus: the family is a set of old twins. Leraar and arts show a Dutch quirk: professions after zijn drop the article. Mijn moeder is leraar, not een leraar.

pattern.title: Profession without an article
pattern.content: Mijn moeder is leraar, mijn vader is arts, mijn broer is bakker. After zijn, an unmodified profession takes no een. The family words keep their articles.
pattern.trap_note: Do not say mijn moeder is een leraar in this frame. Dutch drops the indefinite article before an unmodified profession.

exercises.prompt: Match each English meaning with its Dutch twin (Moeder, Vader & Leraar):
exercises.target_answer: de moeder, de vader, de broer, de zus, de leraar, de arts
exercises.meaning: mother, father, brother, sister, teacher, doctor
exercises.explanation: These are the anchors of "Moeder, Vader & Leraar": read each Dutch form through the pattern, not as a new word.

exercises.prompt: Which sentence says: “My mother is a teacher.”?
exercises.explanation: “Mijn moeder is leraar.” is the Dutch form; the other readings bend the pattern of “Moeder, Vader & Leraar”.

cues: The pattern: Profession without an article
It means: My father is a doctor.
exercises.explanation: “Mijn vader is arts.” puts the thought together the Dutch way — Profession without an article.

diagnosis.slip: an English-shaped word order slipped in
diagnosis.cue: Do not say mijn moeder is een leraar in this frame. Dutch drops the indefinite article before an unmodified profession.

exercises.prompt: Which English sentence is built the Dutch way?
exercises.explanation: “Mijn broer is bakker.” is word-for-word “My brother is baker.”. The odd English is the lesson — never a model to produce. Pattern: Profession without an article.

exercises.prompt: Listen and write the whole sentence.
cues: It means: My sister is here.
exercises.explanation: “Mijn zus is hier.” reuses only material taught in “Moeder, Vader & Leraar” — Profession without an article.
exercises.affirmation: You heard “Mijn zus is hier.” — a sentence built from the lesson's own Dutch, practising Profession without an article.

twist.prompt: One more, no safety net — say: “We are family.”
twist.explanation: Familie is a de-word; the predicate noun takes no article here.

summary.outcome: Name family members and professions, dropping the article after zijn.
summary.takeaway: Dutch profession phrases are a small article rule, not a vocabulary list.
summary.curiosity_teaser: Up next on De Brug: Hand, Voet & Het Blauwe Shirt.

moeder.etymology_derivation: English mother and Dutch moeder are the same word.

vader.etymology_derivation: English father and Dutch vader are the same word with two regular correspondences.

broer.etymology_derivation: English brother and Dutch broer are cognate; Dutch shortened the word.

zus.etymology_derivation: A short form of zuster; English sis is a playful cousin.

leraar.etymology_derivation: From leren ('teach'); the -aar ending marks the agent.

arts.etymology_derivation: From Latin ars ('art, skill'); Dutch narrowed it to physician.
